reading.body:
Verizon Communications and its subsidiaries filed five Lobbying Disclosure Act reports on AI, naming six bills and sixteen lobbyists.

The filings cluster. Eleven lobbyists appear on four or five of the five reports, and five appear on only one. That is the signature of a standing account rather than a one-off push: a core team carries the AI issue across every filing period, and additional names rotate in when a specific bill needs coverage. The six bills named, three Senate and three House, all carry 2025-or-later designations, so this is current activity rather than a historical record.

For AI specifically, the useful fact is that a telecommunications carrier is lobbying on AI at all. Verizon's exposure to AI runs through the physical layer it already owns: the fiber, data centers, and power contracts that training and inference depend on. A firm in that position has reason to care how AI is defined, taxed, and permitted, because those definitions land on infrastructure it operates. The data does not say which bills Verizon supported or opposed, and it does not say what provisions the filings addressed.

What the data does not cover is equally important. It records that a filing names a bill, not what was argued, and it gives no dollar amounts, no committee targets, and no outcomes. Five filings is a small count, and the LDA threshold means smaller or quieter AI lobbying by the same firm would not appear here at all. Read this as evidence of sustained attention to AI legislation by one carrier, not as a measure of influence.
